descripcion: At C1 the focus shifts to verbs where gerund and infinitive both exist but shift the meaning subtly — regret, go on, mean — and to distinguishing perfect gerunds (having done) from simple ones, which mark that an action happened before the main verb.

cuadroReferencia.notaPie: Having done + past participle marks that the gerund's action happened before the main verb: having finished the report, she left.

ejemplos.texto: I regret to say the meeting has been cancelled.
He went on to explain the reasoning behind the decision.
Having finished early, she decided to review it again.

notas: Regret + infinitive is used almost exclusively for formal announcements of bad news; regret + gerund is a genuine personal regret.
Go on + gerund means to continue doing the same thing; go on + infinitive means to move on to something new.
A perfect gerund (having + participle) is a compact way to show that one action clearly preceded another.

contraste.es: Spanish uses the infinitive more generally and does not mark these meaning differences as systematically. Spanish speakers tend to learn these verbs as isolated exceptions, without seeing the pattern that the gerund points to continuity or an earlier action and the infinitive to a next or different step.
contraste.de: German has no gerund, only the zu-infinitive, and marks these meaning differences with different constructions (vergessen, etwas zu tun gegen vergessen, dass man etwas getan hat). German speakers therefore default to the to-infinitive, and the perfect gerund is often calqued from the German perfect infinitive: I regret to have said instead of I regret having said.
contraste.it: Italian marks several of these distinctions with other means: smettere di fare (stop doing) against fermarsi a fare (stop to do), ricordarsi di fare against ricordarsi di aver fatto. The second pair leads to the calque I remember to have done instead of I remember doing, so the perfect gerund needs special attention.
contraste.fr: French marks the difference between remembering an earlier action and a later duty with the perfect infinitive (se souvenir d'avoir fait). Translated literally, regretter d'avoir dit becomes I regret to have said instead of I regret having said, so the perfect gerund is the main point for French speakers.
contraste.pt: Portuguese marks several of these distinctions lexically: continuar a fazer (go on doing) against passar a fazer (go on to do). The perfect infinitive (lembro-me de ter feito) leads to the calque I remember to have done instead of I remember doing.

errores: Using regret + infinitive for a genuine personal regret instead of a formal announcement.
Confusing went on doing and went on to do.
Using a simple gerund where a perfect gerund would clarify the sequence of events.

traducciones.de: Ich bedaure sagen zu müssen, dass…

autochequeo: Is regret used correctly for formal announcement versus personal regret?
Is went on followed by the right form for continuation versus a new step?
Is a perfect gerund used where the sequence of events needs clarifying?
Do the subtle meaning shifts match what I actually intend to say?
Are at least five of these nuanced verbs used correctly?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on gerunds and infinitives with a meaning shift: regret, go on, mean, and perfect gerunds. Check whether the chosen form matches the intended meaning. Do not rewrite the text.

it: *ricordarsi di aver fatto* rendered as *remember to have done* instead of *remember doing*.
fr: *avoir l'habitude de* rendered with an infinitive: *I am used to work late* instead of *I am used to working late*.
pt: *lembrar-se de ter feito* rendered as *remember to have done* instead of *remember doing*.
